findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator crashes when used with a datetime sort key, which is how the audit logs endpoint uses it
findings.body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key copies Paginator's numeric implementation: `value = getattr(item, self.key); return int(math.floor(value) ...)`. The endpoint that instantiates it (organization_auditlogs.py) passes `order_by="-datetime"`, so `value` is a `datetime` object and `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime`. build_cursor/_build_next_values call get_item_key on the first result of every page that has results, so every request to the audit logs endpoint with `optimized_pagination=true` (by a superuser or org member with global access) will fail with a 500. DateTimePaginator exists precisely because datetimes need the strftime conversion; OptimizedCursorPaginator omits it. Its value_from_cursor has the matching defect (returns the raw cursor value instead of converting millis back to a datetime like DateTimePaginator does), so the cursor comparison in build_queryset would also be broken.

findings.title: Negative-offset "advanced" slicing raises AssertionError on Django QuerySets; the feature is non-functional
findings.body: When `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start. Django QuerySet slicing does not support negative indices and raises `AssertionError: Negative indices are not allowed` when the queryset is not already evaluated, because there is no SQL equivalent of a negative OFFSET. The comment claiming "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is simply false. Any client that sends a crafted cursor with a negative offset (Cursor.from_string parses user-supplied strings like `0:-5:0` without validation) to an endpoint using this paginator gets a 500 instead of results. The whole 'advanced features' branch either crashes (negative offset) or is a byte-for-byte copy of BasePaginator.get_result with no behavioral difference (normal offsets), so it provides no optimization at all.

findings.title: New `optimized_pagination` query-parameter code path is undocumented and completely untested
findings.body: This PR adds a new, undocumented request parameter (`optimized_pagination=true`) that switches a public (albeit EXPERIMENTAL) endpoint to a different paginator and enables an 'advanced features' mode, gated on `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`. There are no tests for this path anywhere in the PR, no API documentation for the new parameter, and no explanation of what it actually optimizes (the paginator is functionally identical to the default except for a negative-offset branch that crashes — see other findings). The PR description is just 'Test 2', which suggests this change was not reviewed as a deliberate feature. Given the path is broken for its only configured sort key (datetime), the lack of tests is why that was not caught.

findings.title: zunionstore merges use the default AGGREGATE SUM, corrupting scores of payloads present in both keys
findings.body: Both merge operations (`redis.call("zunionstore", set_key, 2, set_key, span_key)` at lines 47 and 53) omit an AGGREGATE argument, so Redis defaults to SUM. When the same span payload exists in both source keys — which happens under Kafka's at-least-once delivery, e.g. a span delivered in one batch lands in the set keyed by its parent while a duplicate delivery in a later batch lands in the merged set — the resulting member's score is the sum of the two end_timestamp_precise values. Since the score is the span's end timestamp used to order the zset, this silently doubles the timestamp. The consequences are that zpopmin eviction (which pops the lowest scores) evicts the wrong spans, and the flush-time iteration order no longer reflects chronological order. The previous sunionstore-based code had no score semantics so this was not an issue; the fix is to pass `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) to both zunionstore calls.

findings.title: New span eviction (zpopmin at 1000) silently drops span data with no metric or log, and can evict the segment's root span
findings.body: The script now evicts the lowest-scored (oldest end_timestamp) members whenever a segment exceeds 1000 spans. Unlike the previous behavior — where oversized segments were skipped at flush time with `metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded")` and an error log — this eviction is completely silent: there is no metric, no log, and no marker on the flushed segment, so the ongoing data loss is invisible to operators. Additionally, if the segment/root span is among the evicted members (possible whenever its end_timestamp is not the maximum, e.g. async traces), the segment is flushed without any root span, so no span gets `is_segment=True`, while the `span-buf:hrs:` key still reads "1" and forces the shorter root timeout. The limit is also hardcoded to 1000 in Lua, diverging from the Python-side `max_segment_spans` config (default 1001), which this PR leaves as a dead, unused parameter in SpansBuffer.__init__ (buffer.py line 150) — so the two limits can drift and the config can no longer be tuned from Python at all.

findings.title: Redirect-following loop reduced from 10000 to 1000 iterations with no justification, silently breaking deep segment trees
findings.body: The loop bound was reduced tenfold and the explanatory comment ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted. If a redirect chain in `span-buf:sr:{...}` exceeds 1000 hops, the loop exits with a stale `set_span_id`, and line 40 then writes an incorrect redirect mapping for the incoming span — the span is attached to the wrong segment and the trace is silently assembled incorrectly. There is no error signal when the cap is hit (redirect_depth is returned but nothing distinguishes 'resolved' from 'gave up'). Reducing the guarantee 10x needs at least a metric/alert on `redirect_depth == 1000` or a comment explaining why 1000 is safe; neither is present, and the diff gives no reason for the change.

findings.title: Direct `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` access will crash the consumer on messages that lack the field
findings.body: process_batch now reads `end_timestamp_precise` with direct dict indexing. The existing consumer test message did not contain this field until this PR added it, which is evidence that messages without the field are representable in the topic (older producers or schema versions, plus any backlog present at deploy time). A KeyError raised inside process_batch propagates out of the RunTask/multiprocessing strategy and kills the consumer, stalling the whole partition — a much worse failure mode than defaulting the score (e.g. `val.get("end_timestamp_precise") or 0` or falling back to the message timestamp). If the field is guaranteed by the current schema, that guarantee should at least be stated; the current code makes any pre-upgrade buffered message fatal.

findings.title: BasePaginator now silently clamps negative non-prev offsets to 0 instead of erroring
findings.body: The base-class change `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` alters behavior for any client that sends a cursor with a negative offset: previously `queryset[offset:stop]` would raise Django's negative-index AssertionError (a clear failure), while now a non-prev cursor with offset < 0 silently returns the first page of results again. A paging client that somehow ends up with a negative offset (or a maliciously crafted cursor) will re-receive page one and can loop over the same data indefinitely instead of surfacing an error. The is_prev branch is left unclamped, so the two paths are inconsistent: prev cursors with negative offsets still crash while next cursors silently reset. If negative offsets are meant to be invalid, both branches should reject them the way OffsetPaginator does with BadPaginationError.

findings.title: Comment claims negative offsets 'enable efficient reverse pagination' but they break the offset arithmetic in this module
findings.body: The new comment on Cursor.offset states that negative offsets enable "efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets". That is not how the module works: _build_next_values and _build_prev_values compute offsets by adding/subtracting the page limit from the current offset, and consumers of these cursors slice querysets where negative offsets are unsupported (raising errors) or silently misbehave. The comment documents a capability that does not exist anywhere in the codebase and will mislead future maintainers into relying on it.
